summary: Defines Robust Header Compression (ROHC) profiles for compressing RTP/UDP-Lite/IP and UDP-Lite/IP packets, based on their differences from the profiles for UDP.

plainLanguage.summary: It shortens the address labels on each packet, the way you abbreviate a long address after you've said it once.

questions: how does rohc compress udp-lite headers
what is the checksum coverage field
subtitle: Two header compression profiles that teach ROHC how to handle UDP-Lite's Checksum Coverage field.

tldr.problem: UDP-Lite replaces the UDP Length field with a Checksum Coverage field that cannot always be inferred, so the existing ROHC profiles for UDP cannot compress it properly. UDP-Lite also has a different protocol identifier.
tldr.mechanism: Profiles 0x0007 (RTP/UDP-Lite/IP) and 0x0008 (UDP-Lite/IP) copy the ROHC UDP profiles and add two context flags and a new Checksum Coverage Extension (CCE) packet type to send the coverage value only when needed.
tldr.outcome: When coverage equals the packet length or stays fixed, UDP-Lite compresses about as well as UDP. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 4815.

today: RFC 4019 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 4815. Read that update alongside this RFC.

sections.title: Why UDP-Lite Needs Its Own Profiles
sections.content:
Robust Header Compression (ROHC) is a framework on which profiles are defined for different protocol sets. It has mostly focused on IP/UDP/RTP headers, which are large compared with the small payloads that voice over IP often carries. ROHC RTP can compress those headers down to a total size of one octet.

UDP-Lite is a transport protocol similar to UDP for applications that tolerate errors in the payload, where damaged data is better than losing the whole packet. This suits links that can partly damage data, such as wireless links.

Two differences mean UDP profiles cannot simply be reused. UDP-Lite does not share UDP's protocol identifier, and its Checksum Coverage field does not have the semantics of the UDP Length field, so it cannot always be inferred. RFC 4019 defines two profiles as simple modifications of the ROHC UDP profiles in RFC 3095, and also borrows some mechanisms from the ROHC IP-Only profile.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP-Lite is a cousin of UDP with one number that means something different. The shortcut for the old cousin does not quite fit, so this RFC makes a slightly changed shortcut.

sections.title: UDP-Lite and the Checksum Coverage Field
sections.content:
UDP-Lite replaces the UDP Length field with Checksum Coverage, the number of octets covered by the 16-bit checksum. Coverage always includes the UDP-Lite header and may cover the whole packet, in which case UDP-Lite is semantically identical to UDP. Unlike UDP, the UDP-Lite checksum cannot be sent as all zeroes and cannot be disabled for IPv4.

UDP's Length is always redundant, since the link layer can provide it, so compressors send no bits for it. For UDP-Lite the checksum is unpredictable and must always be sent as is. Coverage, in turn, follows one of three patterns across a flow of packets:

  • It changes but always covers the entire packet. This is the UDP-like case, and the value can be INFERRED from the packet length.
  • It stays unchanged, covering up to a fixed boundary. The value is STATIC and can be kept in the context.
  • It changes with no pattern. It is CHANGING and must be sent with every packet.

Any of these may dominate at different times in the life of a flow.
sections.plainLanguage: One number says how much of the letter the check covers. Sometimes it says the whole letter, sometimes always the same part, and sometimes it jumps around. Each case needs a different trick.

sections.title: Design Approach and Context Parameters
sections.content:
Simplicity drives the design. The simplest approach would send Checksum Coverage uncompressed in every packet, but then compression would always be less efficient than for UDP. The RFC aims for similar efficiency to UDP when coverage behaves like UDP Length, so the decompressor needs a way to tell whether the field is present. That is done with a new packet type that uses identifiers left unused in RFC 3095.

The profiles are RTP/UDP-Lite/IP (profile 0x0007) and UDP-Lite/IP (profile 0x0008). Unless stated otherwise they follow ROHC RTP and ROHC UDP. The UDP checksum context parameter is dropped, because the UDP-Lite checksum is always sent in every compressed packet. Two flags are added to the context:

  • CFP (Coverage Field Present): if nonzero, the Checksum Coverage field is carried uncompressed in compressed packets. If zero, it is not sent.
  • CFI (Coverage Field Inferred): used when CFP is zero. If nonzero, coverage is inferred from the packet length. If zero, it is taken from the value stored in the context.

At initialization, CFP MUST be nonzero if coverage differs from the packet length in any IR or IR-DYN packet, and CFI MUST be nonzero if coverage equals the packet length in an IR or IR-DYN packet. In the IR and IR-DYN dynamic part, a 2-octet Checksum Coverage field is added before the Checksum field.
sections.plainLanguage: Two switches tell both sides how to handle the odd number. One says whether it is written down every time, and the other says whether to just assume it means the whole letter.

sections.title: The CCE Packet Type
sections.content:
The general compressed packet format follows the ROHC RTP one, with extra fields for multiple IP headers and for coverage. The Checksum Coverage field (2 octets) is present when CFP is 1 or when the packet type is CCE, followed by the 2-octet Checksum.

The Checksum Coverage Extension (CCE) packet type handles changing coverage patterns. It extends packet types 2, 1 or 0 by replacing the first octet's type identifier with an unused one (111110FK) and moving the original identifier inside. Coverage is always present in a CCE packet. The last two bits, F and K, choose the variant:

  • CCE() updates no context values beyond what the inner packet does. It is mode-agnostic and useful when deviations from the assumed pattern are rare.
  • CCE(ON) sets CFP to a nonzero value, turning on the coverage field. It suits flows where coverage precludes compression.
  • CCE(OFF) sets CFP to zero, updates CFI (nonzero if coverage equals the packet length) and updates the stored coverage. It suits flows that seldom deviate from the assumed pattern.

CCE(ON) and CCE(OFF) MUST NOT extend R-0 and R-1* headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The CCE packet is a special envelope that says, this time I am including the odd number. Variants also flip the switches on or off for future packets.

sections.title: Compressor and Decompressor Behaviour
sections.content:
If CFP is zero and the coverage differs both from the stored context value and from the packet length, the field cannot be compressed. The compressor must then send it using a CCE packet, or re-initialize the context with an IR packet. When CFP is zero, the decompressor takes coverage from the context if CFI is zero, and otherwise infers it from the packet length provided by the IP module.

The profiles add three further mechanisms taken from the ROHC IP-Only profile. First, the compressor may decline a mode transition by redefining Mode value 0 as Cancel; the decompressor MUST then stay in its current mode. Second, a CONTEXT_MEMORY feedback option (type 9, length 0) tells the compressor that the decompressor lacks memory for the context, so the compressor SHOULD compress in a way that needs less memory or stop compressing. Third, a Static IP Identifier (SID) flag lets a constant IP-ID be compressed away, and only IR and IR-DYN packets can update it.
sections.plainLanguage: If the odd number is what both sides expect, nothing is sent. If it is not, the sender uses the special envelope or starts over, and the receiver can say it is too full to remember more.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3095 apply integrally to this document, without modification.

IANA reserved ROHC profile identifiers 0x0007 (ROHC RTP/UDP-Lite) and 0x0008 (ROHC UDP-Lite). Identifiers of the form 0xnn07 and 0xnn08 are reserved for future variants.
sections.plainLanguage: It follows the same safety rules as the ROHC it is built on, and it was given two official profile numbers.

fields.name: Checksum Coverage
fields.desc: Octets covered by the checksum; replaces the UDP Length field.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Checksum over the covered part; cannot be sent as all zeroes.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Reserved at framework level for IR-DYN.

items.label: CCE()
items.desc: Updates only what the inner packet type updates.

items.label: CCE(OFF)
items.desc: Sets CFP to zero and updates CFI and stored coverage.
